# v1.0 The Taxidermy Instinct

San Francisco residents who block new housing because it clashes with the city's Victorian character are not defending history. They're mounting it.

Taxidermy is a real craft, and it's instructive here. A taxidermist keeps the hide, the shape, the glass eyes set at exactly the angle the living animal held its gaze. What a taxidermist cannot keep is the animal. The thing on the wall looks like it, right down to the whiskers, but nothing inside it is alive anymore.

That is what a historic district does to a neighborhood.

The Victorians people fight to protect in San Francisco were themselves the disruption — mass-produced speculative housing thrown up fast to house a boom, on land that had a life on it long before any of them were framed. Freezing a city at 1895, or 1950, or 1980, isn't honoring history. It's picking one frame out of a very long film and mounting it as the only true one.

The West Village is the finished version of this experiment. Its cobblestones, its low brick rowhouses, its wrought iron are close to untouched since the historic district went up decades ago. The hide is perfect. What's gone is the animal: the Beat poets, the folk clubs, the Stonewall-era radicals, the working artists who could once afford a lease on nothing. They didn't leave because the neighborhood changed. They left because it stopped being allowed to.

A museum piece doesn't die twice.

Nobody voting to preserve that skin thinks of themselves as a taxidermist. They think of themselves as a curator, saving something fragile from something crude. That belief costs them nothing to hold, because the law lets a room full of homeowners impose their preference for how a street should look on people who will never get to live there. If liking techno music let you ban every other genre in the city, you'd take that deal too.

None of this makes them liars. The taste is sincere, the nostalgia is sincere, the belief that the shell has value in itself is sincere — and that's exactly the problem, because a sincere belief never has to check its own results. The people priced out of the neighborhood aren't a rebuttal to the preservationist; they're invisible to the frame the preservationist is using.

The stuffed animal still has glass eyes. It has stopped looking at anything.
